recentItems.title: Kentucky farm rears ostriches as alternative meat for allergy sufferers
recentItems.description:
(6 Sep 2026) 
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Danville, Kentucky, US -- 18 August 2026

1. W.D. King feeding ostriches at Alpha Roost farm
2. Close pan of ostrich heads
3. Adult ostriches in a field
4. SOUNDBITE (English): W.D. King, Kentucky ostrich farmer: 
“I've been in poultry nutrition work most of my life in research, as a job, and then raised beef cattle here on the farm. And I kind of started joking that ostrich,  you know, I’ll start raising ostriches that's what we'll do. And opened my mouth to the wrong fella, I was talking to Brent one day, he had the same question, what are you going to do? I said, ah, you know, I'll just raise ostriches. And he said, if you're serious, I'm in.”

5. W.D. King standing near large ostrich
6. Ostrich heads going up and down
7. Close on feeding ostriches
8 . SOUNDBITE (English): W.D. King, Kentucky ostrich farmer: 
“Alpha-gal is the main driver. That is what's driving the ostrich market. It does not,  the ostrich meat, because it's a bird, not a mammal, doesn't contain the alpha-gal molecule, so you can safely eat that meat without reaction, and it's very much like a steak.”

9. W.D. King driving egg collection vehicle
10. Close of an ostrich foot
11. Baby ostriches in hatchery
12. W.D. King and Brent Williams looking over hatchery
13. Package of ground ostrich meat
14. Pan of Dry Branch Farm Market
15. Close of Dry Branch sign
16. SOUNDBITE (English): Leah Gibbs, ostrich meat vendor in Kentucky: 
“It's staggering how many people are getting diagnosed with alpha-gal or are affected by it either themselves or somebody that they know. So we have people that drive here from all over the state to get the ostrich. They are elated to have something that is an alternative to beef. It is safe for them with their allergy, but it also is full of flavour. I mean, it tastes exactly like beef.”

17. Shelf of ostrich meat products
18. Leah Gibbs serving a customer

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Louisville, Kentucky, US -- 28 August 2026

19. Exterior University of Louisville Hospital emergency entrance
20. Chart on the wall in the medical room
21. SOUNDBITE (English) Dr Martin Huecker, emergency room doctor: 
“Yes, so it's an interesting allergy because often we're allergic to proteins from food, but in this case it's a carbohydrate, like a sugar, that's in mammalian products, meats, you know, gelatine, that kind of stuff and so people get sensitized to it by ticks, typically by a tick bite, and they will actually become allergic to all these mammalian products because their body's trying to attack that sugar that the tick kind of introduced to our system.”

ASSOCIATED PRESS
New York, US -- 28 May 2026

 “Yes, it’s increasing. You know, tick bite and tick exposure is increasing in general, and because that's the vector for us to get this allergy, yes, like that's a lot of people are saying it is increasing all throughout the country, but certainly in pockets.”

recentItems.title: Far-right AfD candidate Siegmund casts vote in Saxony-Anhalt election
recentItems.description:
(6 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Tangermünde, Germany - 6 September 2026
1. Various of Ulrich Siegmund and Julia Siegmund arriving on motorbike, crowd cheering
2. Siegmund greeting and talking to supporters
3. Siegmund posing for selfie with supporter
4. Siegmund greeting and talking to supporters
5. Various of Siegmund giving thumbs up to supporters, crowd cheering
6. Ulrich and Julia Siegmund entering polling station
7. Close of press photographers
8. Ulrich and Julia Siegmund receiving election materials
9. Close of ballot box
10. Ulrich and Julia Siegmund casting votes
11. Ulrich and Julia Siegmund leaving polling station
12. Siegmund arriving for statement, crowd chanting
13. Soundbite (German) Ulrich Siegmund, AfD candidate for Saxony-Anhalt:
"So, what we’re experiencing here right now—when was the last time we saw something like this in German history, something so positive? A positive outlook on politics? You can see how many people here are filled with hope. And the atmosphere we have here is just absolutely, absolutely wonderful. A spirit of optimism—that’s Vision 2026. I don’t know of any other party where things look the way they do here today in Tangermünde. And these are the images this country needs, that it’s moving forward again, that we have a sense of optimism, that we’re standing together again, that we’re bridging divides—that’s definitely what I want to do after the election. We have to stand together again. It’s incredibly important. And this day begins right here and now, on the 6th of the 9th, in Saxony-Anhalt."
14. Close of Siegmund on camera screen
15. Siegmund surrounded by press teams
16. Siegmund and wife putting on helmets
17. Siegmund turning motorbike around for leaving
18. Various of Ulrich and Julia Siegmund leaving on motorbike
STORYLINE:
Far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) candidate Ulrich Siegmund cast his ballot Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt’s state election in his hometown of Tangermünde with his wife Julia.

A group of supporters gathered outside the polling station and cheered as Siegmund arrived and cast his vote.

The vote for the state legislature in Saxony-Anhalt, a region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin, has gained outsized prominence because it represents the best chance yet of a governor’s post for the far-right, anti-migration AfD.

Siegmund is seeking to lead the state government if his party wins an absolute majority.

"I don’t know of any other party where things look the way they do here today in Tangermünde," Siegmund said outside the polling station. "And these are the images this country needs, that it’s moving forward again, that we have a sense of optimism, that we’re standing together again."

Such a result could overcome the so-called “firewall” of mainstream parties’ refusal to work with the AfD and pave the way for Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II.

The AfD is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous eastern states and is seeking what would be the biggest political prize in the party’s 13-year history.

Siegmund has said he would only seek election as governor by state lawmakers if the AfD wins an absolute majority.

AP video shot by: Daniel Niemann and Fanny Brodersen

recentItems.title: US envoys Kushner and Witkoff arrive in Kyiv in a renewed push to end Russia’s war
recentItems.description:
(6 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Kyiv, Ukraine - 6 September 2026
1. Various of U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arriving and being greeted by officials
2. Witkoff and Kushner walking
STORYLINE:
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday in their first official visit to Ukraine as part of a renewed push for peace after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 

Their trip follows a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, seeking to revive peace talks during escalating aerial attacks by both sides. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday that Kyiv is ready for a “constructive” discussion with U.S. representatives.

“We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared,” he said in a post on Telegram.

Saturday's meeting in Moscow lasted more than three hours behind closed doors and ended without announcements of any breakthroughs. 

Putin’s foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, described them afterward as constructive, frank, and useful but didn’t discuss specific outcomes.

While Moscow offered its “comprehensive assessment” of the battlefield situation in Ukraine, Ushakov said, the talks were not purely focused on the war in Ukraine.

AP video shot by: Vasilisa Stepanenko

recentItems.title: Tension high at Israel-Lebanon border following deadly IDF attacks in south Lebanon
recentItems.description:
(6 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTIONS SUMMARY

++PLEASE NOTE THIS MATERIAL WAS SHOT BY AN AP VIDEOGRAPHER. THE AP SUBMITTED THE MATERIAL TO THE ISRAELI MILITARY CENSOR, WHICH DID NOT MADE DELETIONS ++

ASSOCIATED PRESS   
Northern Israel - 6 September 2026
1. Military jeeps driving at Israeli Lebanese border
2. Various of parked tanks and APCs on the Israeli side of the Lebanese border
3. Military jeeps driving at Israeli Lebanese border
4. Jeeps entering Lebanon
5. Border wall, Beaufort castle in background, AUDIO of gunfire
6. House in Lebanon seen from the Israeli side, audio of gunfire
7. Israeli army post
8. Various of UN post
9. Various of Beaufort castle and destruction in south Lebanon seen from the Israeli side of the border
10. Various of border
11. Various of destruction in south Lebanon seen from the Israeli side of the border
12. Various of bullet holes in bulletproof glass, Lebanese border in background
13. Top shot of Metula, south Lebanon in background
STORYLINE:
Tensions were high on Sunday at the Israeli-Lebanese border as Israel struck southern Lebanon after issuing a rare evacuation warning.

The Israeli military said its latest strikes came in response to a drone attack launched earlier on Sunday by Hezbollah on Israeli troops in southern Lebanon. 

No soldiers were injured, it said. 

The Israeli strikes on the Lebanese village of Arabsalim killed two, the Lebanese health ministry said. 

Another two were killed in the city of Nabatiyeh. 

Since a ceasefire went into effect between Israel and Hezbollah more than two months ago, fighting has subsided in much of Lebanon, and Israeli evacuation warnings have become rare. 

But fighting has continued around a strategic hill near the city of Nabatiyeh. 

On Thursday, Israel’s military announced it had taken “operational control” of the Ali Taher hill and a network of tunnels beneath it that Hezbollah uses to shelter its fighters and weapons.

The latest Israel-Hezbollah war began when Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel days after Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28. 

Israel invaded Lebanon and has since occupied a large swath of its south.

AP video shot by: Alon Bernstein

recentItems.title: Israeli airstrikes on southern Lebanon kill 4 people and wound 20 others
recentItems.description:
(6 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTIONS SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Arabsalim, Lebanon - 6 September 2026
1. Various of bulldozer removing rubble and searching for people trapped underneath.
2. Body being recovered from the rubble.. 
3. Various of damage to targeted house as bulldozers continue searching through rubble
4. Various of damage to another house adjacent to  targeted house
5. Various of interior of house showing damage and rubble
6. Hole in side of wall, rubble outside
7. Various of damage and rubble, house owner's relatives checking pointing at debris 
8. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Imad Ali Hassan, resident of Arabsalim and uncle of owner of targeted house: 
“The young man, the owner of this house, forty years ago, he emigrated and started from scratch. Every penny he earned, he had sent back to his family so they could build this house for him here. He used to come back to check on it, happy to have his dream home that he wanted to build. He was dreaming about it while living in Canada.” 
9. Wide of damaged house 
10. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Imad Ali Hassan, resident of Arabsalim and uncle of owner of targeted house: 
“Whatever the Israelis may try to do, we will remain steadfast. Wherever we are, even if we are living abroad, this is our village, the South is our home, and Lebanon is our country. It is out of our love for Lebanon that we have reached this point.”
11. Wide of smoke rising due to Israeli shelling on  neighbouring village of Kfar Rumman
STORYLINE:
Lebanon's Health Ministry said at least four people were killed on Sunday in Israeli strikes in villages in Nabatiyeh province, in southern Lebanon. 

Two were killed in Arabsalim, where Israel also struck a residential house after issuing a warning. 

Another two were killed in Nabatiyeh Fawqa. 

At least 20 others were wounded, the ministry said, among them three children and five women. 

Footage from the village of Arabsalim shows three houses damaged, including two that were completely destroyed and a third that sustained partial damage. 

A body was recovered from the rubble of one of the damaged houses , as rescue and recovery operations continued.

One of Israel's strikes had apparently struck the Ghandour Hospital in Nabatiyeh Fawqa, though the province's civil defense told The Associated Press that the medical facility had been emptied out like much of the town due to the war. 

 Since a ceasefire went into effect between Israel and Hezbollah more than two months ago, fighting has stopped in much of Lebanon, but not on a strategic hill overlooking parts of Nabatiyeh.

13. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Antonella Molina, aunt of missing Andrés Molina:
"We are finding a way to find him because many people say they have seen him. Of 100 people I have asked about him, 85 say they have seen him. And they all give the same description: with a t-shirt, shorts, dirty, he is walking disoriented. So we have the hope he is around."
14. Antonella Molina and Pedro Gomez, cousin of Andrés Molina, walking through destroyed neighborhood

20. Mid of damaged building
21. SOUNDBITE (Spanish) Pedro Gómez, cousin of missing Andrés Molina:
"Well, two months after the earthquake we feel hopeful to find Andres. At least people have given us proof of life, several people we know and people around this area. And well, today we are trying to get closer to his whereabouts."
22. Gómez and Antonella Molina walking by collapsed building
23. Various of Gómez and Antonella Molina placing flyer on post outside business
24. Antonella Molina and Gómez speaking with local resident

26. Antonella Molina grabbing torn flyer from place she believed he has been sleeping UPSOUND Antonella Molina (Spanish): "Look, one of his flyers"
27. Antonella Molina showing torn flyers on wall UPSOUND Antonella Molina (Spanish): "Look, the other person’s flyer is intact, but his is torn. I feel it might be him breaking it"
28. Close of broken flyer 
STORYLINE:
Antonella Molina, her nephew Pedro Molina and a group of friends set out at 8 a.m. on a recent Saturday, hands full of flyers, walking carefully through the rubble that remains throughout La Guaira after two catastrophic back-to-back earthquakes 10 weeks ago. 

Their mission is to find 18-year-old Andrés Molina - Antonella’s nephew and Pedro’s cousin - who they haven’t heard from since the double earthquakes hit Venezuela on June 24. 

Andrés is among tens of thousands who remain missing, according to an independent account, far surpassing the government estimate of 1,500.


The building once housed more than 30 people but there was no sign of Andrés, not even the backpack he always carried.








But Andrés was never there when they showed up.

recentItems.title: German region votes in election that could bring first far-right state governor to power
recentItems.description:
(6 Sep 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Magdeburg, Germany - 6 September 2026
1. Wide of voters registering at polling station 
2. Close up of ballot box label reading (German): "State Election" 
3. Wide of voter inside polling booth 
4. Close up of voter placing ballot into ballot box 
5. Wide of election officials inside polling station
6. SOUNDBITE (German) Joachim Meier, Magdeburg voter:
“Yes, we hope that our vote—or my vote—will have some impact in ensuring that the balance of power in the state parliament is such that we prevent the others, who are currently so far ahead, from coming to power. That is my honest opinion, and that is why I voted tactically.”
7. Wide of voter entering polling station 
8. SOUNDBITE (German) Jörg Schulz, Magdeburg voter:
“(My expectation is) for things to move in the right direction, I have to say quite honestly. And the citizens will decide how things proceed from here.”
9. Mid of voter standing at polling booth
10. Wide of voters casting ballots 
11. SOUNDBITE (German) Doreen Hoffmann, Magdeburg voter:
“Not many (expectations). I don’t think there are any winners in this election. There was far too much violence from both sides leading up to it. And I hope that people will retain and rediscover their dignity and what unites us. That would be important to me.”
12. Mid of election officials assisting voter
13. Mid of hand placing ballot into ballot box
14. Mid of voters casting ballots
15. Mid of voter placing ballot into ballot box
16. Wide of voters checking in at polling station
STORYLINE:
Polls opened in a regional election in eastern Germany on Sunday that could bring to power the first far-right state government in the nation’s post-World War II history.

Voters of various age groups were seen coming early to cast their votes. 

The vote for the state legislature in Saxony-Anhalt, a region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin, has gained outsized prominence because it represents the best chance yet of a governor’s post for the far-right, anti-migration Alternative for Germany, or AfD. 

“Yes, we hope that our vote—or my vote—will have some impact in ensuring that the balance of power in the state parliament is such that we prevent the others, who are currently so far ahead, from coming to power. That is my honest opinion, and that is why I voted tactically," said  Joachim Meier, a Magdeburg resident.

If AfD wins, that would be the biggest prize in the party’s 13-year history, at a time when there’s widespread discontent with an unpopular national government that has yet to persuade voters it can get the country’s sluggish economy moving. 

It would be at least a symbolic blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose center-right party has led Saxony-Anhalt for 24 years.

“(My expectation is) for things to move in the right direction, I have to say quite honestly. And the citizens will decide how things proceed from here," said Jörg Schulz, another Magdeburg resident. 

AfD is the biggest opposition party in Germany’s national parliament and is strongest in the formerly communist and less prosperous east, where Saxony-Anhalt is located. Its candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, declares that “we will write history here.”

Despite consistently strong support, though, its chances of taking power are uncertain even if it finishes well ahead of its opponents.


AfD vehemently rejects accusations of extremism.

Jubb'adin, Qalamoun area, Syria - 4 September 2026
1. Various of grooms walking to the wedding venue among a procession that includes dancers, fire-blowers, and men holding a large Syrian flag

6. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Hassan Ammoush, one of the grooms:
“This mass wedding saved us a lot of money, and as they say: 'the hand of God is with the many'. Everyone took part and did more than they had to. This is really good, and I wish it would happen all over Syria, not just in our area. It helps a lot financially and in every way."

7. Various of dancers performing

10. Various of the grooms dancing during mass wedding
11. Close on Ammoush dancing 
12. Various of grooms dancing and celebrating, some carried on shoulders of family members 
13. SOUNDBITE (Arabic) Muhammad Issa, Jabaadeen Deputy Mayor: 
“The idea was to help the grooms and encourage men to get married and to build a better family life.” 

12. Various wides of the tent where the celebrations are taking place, UPSOUND: A famous song in Syria, first sung by rebel icon Abdelbaset Sarout, who was called the"singer of the revolution"
STORYLINE:
Thirty-four grooms celebrated their weddings together in northern rural Damascus on Friday, reviving a tradition that brings families together, while helping ease the cost of marriage.

The village of Jubb'adin in the Qalamoun area was buzzing with music and dancing, as the grooms and their families gathered for the shared celebration.

People cheered for the grooms, who danced in a circle, and then were lifted on shoulders of friends and families as they celebrated. 

Group weddings are an old tradition in parts of Syria, dating back to before the country's 14-years war. 

The idea is to help young couples and their families reduce the expenses associated with holding separate wedding celebrations, at a time when many Syrians are facing economic hardship.

"This is really good and I wish it would happen all over Syria, not just in our area. It helps a lot financially and in every way," said one of the grooms. 

The mass wedding had the many hallmarks of a Damascene celebration, including a A'arada band, which performs a traditional music and dance procession, escorting the grooms to the venue. 

AP video by Abdulrahman Shaheen

STORYLINE:
For almost a year, Randa al-Mansour, a 31-year-old Sudanese housewife, has relied on solar energy panels installed on the rooftop of her building to survive the recurrent blackouts triggered by the war-torn country’s deteriorating electricity grid.

She said it was the only way to manage the recurrent blackouts triggered by the war-torn country’s deteriorating electricity grid.

“We are suffering big time,” said al-Mansour, who lives with her three children in Omdurman, just outside the capital of Khartoum.

"When the children go to school in the morning, they leave while the electricity is out. They find no electricity at the school either, so they are forced to head back home, where there is none too. It is very hard for them to study under such a high temperature," she said.

The Sudanese military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have been fighting since April 2023, killing at least 59,000 people, though aid groups say the number could be higher and displacing some 13 million.
